content:
What would people think about setting up a 'Lean community award' program to recognize outstanding contributions to the Lean community? Doesn't have to have money attached to it, but it might be a way for the community to say thank you to the individuals how make a (maybe unsung) contribution to the whole community.

Obviously if people think this is a good idea, there would be details to be worked out.

"The road to hell is paved with good intentions."

I can imagine this might have undesirable side effects (envy, jealousy, greed) if not handled carefully. If it is built carefully, saying exactly what the intention is (e.g. "we think it important to recognize contributors on an individual basis, to help morale and build community") and if it is clear that the goal is to do this regularly {e.g. "hey guys, we have 57 people to thank this quarter and another hundred by the end of the year, how about making award night on Thursdays and Mondays?") then it becomes clear that most people who deserve the recognition will get it, and it is just a matter of waiting until that recognition comes.

Or maybe the intent is to just acknowledge good contributions or recent developers. The terms of the recognition should be made clear, so as to avoid competing for such recognition. I'm not saying "Don't do it": I'm saying "Tread carefully with much forethought."

content: (As a side note, us newcomers appreciate good examples even more. If someone had a "Lean Pearls" column, like Jon Bentley's Programming Pearls, I would be a faithful reader. I can see an award category for good examples, which might involve less politics and have fewer side effects.)

content: @J. J. Issai (project started by GRP) Totally agreed regarding treading carefully. The last thing I think we would want is that it became a competition etc - the risk of that coming true may be too high, I just don't know.

I remember seeing a previous discussion about whether there could be monetary prizes for people who completed small parts of various high profile proofs. At that time the response was mainly that to paraphrase "the kind of people who want to contribute to MathLib are not the kind of people who are doing it for the fame and money. But doing it for the love of math, the experience and the citation". And basically that it was too difficult and time consuming to sort out the paperwork for such a thing. Plus the amounts of money involved in the scheme of things is not that high.

Now, this is a fair point, and makes sense in that time period where academia is indeed a lowly paid profession. But in this time where the (as you phrased it) elite-athletes are setting up or joining companies, start-ups and riding the AI boom, I think the dynamics have changed a lot. People are happy to contribute and volunteer to a project when it is an all-in-it-together mentality. But when people begin to feel their work is being exploited for other companies or people's fame and fortune it can become a problem. (Obviously not for those who already are well established or don't care about fame and fortune).

How might we solve this dilemma and keep everyone happy?

Well, indeed, I think that the situtation has changed to such a degree that the unpaid volunteer model should be questioned. My suggestion would be not an award system decided on by human hands. But an automated system where a proposition is on a website with a prize money attached. Anyone can submit a proof to the website which is checked automatically and then if it is correct they immediately unlock the prize money. (Now some details may have to be worked out if we also want elegant proofs *see below.)

Whoever gets the prize would be directed to a page where they can fill in their name and photo so they get the credit and fame as well as the money.

Humans could submit propositions for people to solve. Companies can submit prize money. A sort of Kaggle for proofs.

That would be my suggestion. It would solve 4 problems:
(1) Prize money to motivate people
(2) Automatic creditation and fame on the website
(3) Automatic proof checking
(4) Takes humans out of the loop to avoid bias.

I was thinking of setting up this website myself, but I think I would only be able to afford about £5000 of prize money and that probably wouldn't motivate many people. Also, hosting the Lean checker might be expensive. But if no-one runs with this idea I will make this myself and offer cash prizes. [If I can think of a good way to automate that - perhaps Amazon vouchers?]

(This idea might not be suitable exactly for the MathLib but the successful proofs submitted might perhaps speed up the process?) The users would also be able to submit alternative "more elegant" proofs. They wouldn't win prize money, but users could vote on the most elegant, perhaps. (Details to be decided :) ) [In the dream model one could have submitted proofs reference other submitted proofs but that is for the distant future]

I think the question of a bounty system is a related but different topic, which has its own benefits and complications which as you say have been discussed extensively elsewhere.

Going back to the community awards type thing, something like this actually use to exist through Microsoft

https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/academic-program/microsoft-research-lean-award-program/

As far as I am aware this no longer runs.

Yeah, the reason I brought up the bounty idea is just to contrast it with awards. Just because personally I have never really been in favour of human-bestowed awards. (Which might sound strange coming from an Englishman where we have he honours system!) :thinking:

If we could figure out some predetermined metric which could be decided before-hand such as "most lines of code submitted" then it takes it out of subjective decision of small groups of humans.

To me, I am interested in proof checkers precisely because it takes out the subjectivity of whether something is right or wrong. So to me an award system built on a subjective basis would be antithetical to this.

So some way of rewarding top contributors (or even smaller contributors), I would be in favour of, but only if we can somehow take the subjectivity out of it. Which is quite hard to do when people have different ideas of what an elegant contribution might be. Perhaps a voting system for the nominees? But even that has dificulties.

Maybe we could come up with some metrics by which the awards could be judged?
